On May 12, JMOD🇯🇵 spokesperson rejected the 🇨🇳's claim that Tokyo breached its exclusively defense-oriented policy through a Type-88 SSM live-fire drill in the Philippines: https://t.co/rXHFHFrCdy.
He argued the SSMs are intended to counter invading enemies, making the criticism unfounded.

■Translation:

Reporter:

I would like to ask about remarks issued by China’s Ministry of National Defense. A spokesperson for the Chinese Ministry of National Defense claimed, in relation to the U.S.-Philippine-led Balikatan exercise, that Japan and the Philippines are strengthening military collusion and worsening regional tensions, and that Japan dispatched troops to participate in joint exercises, fired offensive missiles overseas for the first time, and deliberately broke through the principle of exclusively defense-oriented policy. Could you share the JMOD spokesperson’s view regarding these remarks?

JMOD Spokesperson:

Regarding the claim that Japan and the Philippines are strengthening military collusion and worsening regional tensions, first of all, with respect to the multinational exercise “Balikatan 26,” this is a multinational exercise co-hosted by the United States and the Philippines. 

For the JMOD and the JSDF, the purpose of participating in this exercise is to maintain and enhance joint operational capabilities, as well as to strengthen cooperation with the Philippines and other participating countries, including the United States, Australia, Canada, France, and New Zealand. 
It is not intended with any specific country or region in mind.

Furthermore, defense cooperation between Japan and the Philippines is conducted with transparency and is aimed at strengthening the deterrence capabilities of both countries and the region. It is not something that heightens regional tensions; rather, it contributes to securing regional peace and stability.

There was also the claim that Japan dispatched troops to participate in joint exercises, fired offensive missiles overseas for the first time, and deliberately broke through the principle of exclusively defense-oriented policy. 

Regarding this point, since the end of the war, Japan has consistently adhered to an exclusively defense-oriented policy under the Constitution of Japan and followed the basic policy of not becoming a military power that poses a threat to other countries, while walking the path of a peace-loving nation.

Under this approach, Japan has deployed and operated the Type 88 surface-to-ship guided missile for as long as 35 years, with the purpose of responding to enemy vessels invading our country. Live-fire training has also been repeatedly conducted in both the United States and Australia.

Japan’s position has remained consistent, and the recent remarks by the Chinese side are not based on facts.

In addition, Article 9 of the Constitution does not deny Japan’s inherent right of self-defense possessed as a sovereign state, and it is permitted to exercise the minimum necessary level of force for self-defense. 

Accordingly, maintaining and improving joint operational capabilities through various training activities, strengthening cooperation with participating countries, and exercising defense capabilities only when Japan comes under armed attack — namely, the exclusively defense-oriented policy, which refers to a passive defense strategy posture — are in no way contradictory.

At a time when unilateral attempts to change the status quo by force or coercion are being observed in the East China Sea and the South China Sea, the most important thing is to maintain regional peace and stability through dialogue and cooperation.

Going forward, Japan will continue to make unwavering efforts toward maintaining and strengthening a free and open international order based on the rule of law, without ever changing its path as a peace-loving nation. That is all.

STATEMENT OF LAW DEANS AND PROFESSORS
ON THE ACCOUNTABILITY OF THE VICE-PRESIDENT

We, the undersigned law deans and law professors, wish:

1. To laud the courageous Members of the House of Representatives who voted to impeach Vice-President Sarah Z. Duterte on the grounds, factual and legal, articulated in the Report of the Committee on Justice;

2. To decry the brazen attempts of members of the Senate to forestall the impeachment trial of the Vice-President, first, by voting for a change of leadership on the eve of the transmittal of the Articles of Impeachment to the Senate, and, second, apparently deciding to adopt the “Escudero definition” of “forthwith” – which, at that unfortunate time, meant, “when it pleased the Senate President”;

3. To remind the Senators that refusing to sit as a Court of Impeachment is not a constitutional option, considering that Article XI, Section 3, paragraphs 3 and 4 are clear that when at least one-third of the Membership of the House of Representatives EITHER votes in affirmance of the Committee Report OR files the Impeachment Complaint, these constitute the Articles of Impeachment and trial “forthwith” proceeds – the clear intendment of the Constitution being that “trial proceeds as a matter of course”;

4. To invite attention of the Members of Senate – as well as the Filipino people – that refusal of public officers to perform a duty imposed by law, particularly by the Constitution, constitutes dereliction of duty that is administratively actionable and conferring an undue advantage and benefit on a person not entitled to it is an indictable criminal offense under Republic Act No. 3019;

5. To urge our law enforcers to cooperate with international legal processes so that, in case the State should so decide in accordance with the relevant provisions of Republic Act No. 9851, Mr. Bato de la Rosa, be made to stand trial before the International Criminal Court at The Hague.

6. To rally all Filipinos to see to the faithful compliance by all public officers of their sworn duty to uphold the Constitution and to abide by the Rule of Law.

#SciFeature 𝗪𝗛𝗘𝗥𝗘 𝗔𝗥𝗘 𝗢𝗨𝗥 𝗠𝗔𝗡𝗚𝗥𝗢𝗩𝗘𝗦? 🌱

Mangrove ecosystems play a crucial role in conserving biodiversity, supporting local communities with essential goods and services, and helping to reduce the impacts of climate change. The map below shows the extent of mangrove forests in the Philippines as of 2020.

According to the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), the country had an estimated 3,114 square kilometers of mangrove forests in 2020. These areas are home to more than 33 species of true mangroves that sustain and enrich the ecosystem.

Most of the remaining mangrove forests are found in the provinces of Palawan (604.6 sq. km), Sulu (260.1 sq. km), Quezon (197.4 sq. km), Tawi-Tawi (151.2 sq. km), Surigao del Norte (140.8 sq. km), Bohol (129.8 sq. km), and Zamboanga Sibugay (126.8 sq. km), based on DENR data.

Mangroves provide a wide range of benefits. Their dense root systems act as natural defenses, shielding coastal communities from storm surges, erosion, and flooding. They also serve as vital nurseries for many marine species, supporting fisheries and the livelihoods that depend on them. In addition, mangroves help combat climate change by storing carbon and improving water quality by filtering pollutants.

Despite their importance, mangrove forests face serious threats, from deforestation due to development and aquaculture to pollution and the effects of climate change, such as rising sea levels and extreme weather. Protecting these ecosystems requires strong conservation efforts, including the establishment of protected areas, community-led initiatives, and sustainable management practices.

Empowering local communities and integrating mangrove conservation into broader coastal planning is key to preserving these ecosystems. Recognizing their value and taking concrete action today is essential to ensuring a resilient future for both nature and people. #OceanMonth #mangroves #Philippines

The map below shows the extent of mangrove forests in the Philippines as of 2020. According to the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), the country had an estimated 3,114 square kilometers of mangrove forests in 2020. These areas are home to more than 33 species of true mangroves that sustain and enrich the ecosystem. Most of the remaining mangrove forests are found in the provinces of Palawan (604.6 sq. km), Sulu (260.1 sq. km), Quezon (197.4 sq. km), Tawi-Tawi (151.2 sq. km), Surigao del Norte (140.8 sq. km), Bohol (129.8 sq. km), and Zamboanga Sibugay (126.8 sq. km), based on DENR data. Mangroves provide a wide range of benefits. Their dense root systems act as natural defenses, shielding coastal communities from storm surges, erosion, and flooding. They also serve as vital nurseries for many marine species, supporting fisheries and the livelihoods that depend on them. In addition, mangroves help combat climate change by storing carbon and improving water quality by filtering pollutants. Despite their importance, mangrove forests face serious threats, from deforestation due to development and aquaculture to pollution and the effects of climate change, such as rising sea levels and extreme weather. Protecting these ecosystems requires strong conservation efforts, including the establishment of protected areas, community-led initiatives, and sustainable management practices. Empowering local communities and integrating mangrove conservation into broader coastal planning is key to preserving these ecosystems. Recognizing their value and taking concrete action today is essential to ensuring a resilient future for both nature and people. #OceanMonth #mangroves #Philippines
